title: Seeing Red: The Psychology of Colour
description: What research really says about how colours affect our feelings and behaviour.
instructions: Read the article about colour psychology, then answer the questions. Choose the best answer for each question.

paragraphs.text: Colour surrounds us so constantly that we rarely stop to think about it, yet businesses, designers and architects spend considerable time and money choosing exactly the right shades. The assumption behind these choices is that colour influences how we feel and behave. But how strong is the evidence for this belief, and how much of it is simply popular myth?

Some effects do appear to be supported by research. Red, for example, is often associated with danger and urgency, which may explain why it is used for warning signs and emergency buttons. Several experiments have suggested that seeing red shortly before a test can slightly lower performance, perhaps because the colour unconsciously signals threat. Blue, on the other hand, is frequently linked with calm and trust, which is one reason it appears so often in the logos of banks and technology companies.

However, many of the most confident claims about colour are poorly supported. Popular articles sometimes state that pink walls reduce aggression or that yellow rooms make babies cry, but attempts to repeat such findings have often failed. Psychologists warn that early studies in this field were frequently small, and that striking results tend to be widely reported while later, less exciting research receives little attention.

Another complication is that the meaning of colour is shaped by culture as well as biology. In many Western countries, white is traditionally worn at weddings, whereas in parts of East Asia it has long been associated with mourning. Personal experience matters too: a colour that reminds one person of a happy childhood holiday may have no particular significance for someone else. As a result, it is risky to assume that any colour will produce the same reaction in everyone.

None of this means that colour is unimportant. Context seems to be crucial: the same shade of red that feels exciting on a sports car may feel alarming on a hospital wall. For designers, the most sensible approach is to treat colour as one ingredient among many, testing choices with real users rather than relying on simple rules about what particular colours supposedly mean.

The commercial world nonetheless continues to take colour very seriously. Companies may spend months choosing the colour of a new logo or package, partly because a distinctive shade can make a brand instantly recognisable on a crowded shelf. In this case, the value of colour lies less in any direct effect on emotions than in familiarity: once customers have learned to connect a particular colour with a particular product, they can find it quickly and may trust it more. This is why a sudden change to a well-known brand's colours can confuse loyal customers. Some firms have even tried to protect their signature colours legally, so that competitors cannot copy them.

Colour also interacts with light in ways that are easy to overlook. Even the same paint can look noticeably different on two walls of one room, depending on which way they face. A wall that looks warm and welcoming in the soft light of a showroom may appear dull or cold under harsh office lighting, and natural daylight changes the appearance of colours throughout the day. For this reason, architects designing schools, hospitals and offices often pay as much attention to windows and lamps as to paint. Some researchers argue that access to daylight and views of nature may influence well-being more reliably than the colour of the walls themselves.

Perhaps the most useful lesson from colour research is a general one about how we evaluate claims. Simple, memorable statements, such as 'blue makes you productive', spread easily because they are easy to repeat and seem to offer quick solutions. Real findings, by contrast, are usually more cautious and depend on circumstances. Being aware of this difference does not mean ignoring colour altogether. Rather, it means enjoying and using it thoughtfully, while remaining a little sceptical whenever someone promises that a single shade will transform the way we think or feel.

questions.text: What is the main idea of the article?
options: Colour can affect us, but its effects are less simple and universal than is often claimed.
Red is the most powerful colour in design.
Colour has no effect at all on human behaviour.
All banks should use blue in their logos.
questions.explanation: The writer accepts some effects of colour but shows that many claims are weak and that culture and context matter.

evidence.quote: how much of it is simply popular myth
None of this means that colour is unimportant.

questions.text: What have experiments suggested about seeing red before a test?
options: It improves concentration.
It may slightly reduce performance.
It makes people feel calm.
It has no measurable effect.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says seeing red can slightly lower test performance.

evidence.quote: seeing red shortly before a test can slightly lower performance

questions.text: In paragraph 2, the word "unconsciously" is closest in meaning to:
options: very loudly
on purpose
without a person being aware of it
only occasionally

evidence.quote: the colour unconsciously signals threat

questions.text: Why does the writer mention pink walls and yellow rooms?
options: To recommend colours for children's bedrooms
To show that research on colour is always reliable
To explain why babies cry
To give examples of popular claims that lack strong evidence
questions.explanation: These are examples of confident claims that later studies often failed to repeat.

evidence.quote: many of the most confident claims about colour are poorly supported

questions.text: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about how research is reported?
options: Small studies are always more accurate than large ones.
Psychologists refuse to study colour.
The public may hear more about surprising findings than about later studies that question them.
Journalists report only boring results.
questions.explanation: Striking results are widely reported, while later, less exciting research is largely ignored.

evidence.quote: striking results tend to be widely reported while later, less exciting research receives little attention

linked with mourning
considered lucky
used for warning signs

questions.text: What does the example of the sports car and the hospital wall show?
options: The same colour can create different feelings depending on where it is used.
Red should never be used in hospitals.

Most people dislike the colour red.

It is linked with calm and trust.
It signals danger and urgency.
It is especially popular with young customers.

It disappears once customers know the brand well.
